title: Session-splinter latency vs cost — algorithmic annotated draft
content:
Purpose

Quick exploratory draft: quantify latency and $/q impacts when routing short, interactive sessions to lightweight micro-shards ("session-splinter" routing) vs our baseline multiplexed slots. This is intentionally rough — goal is to capture the shape of tradeoffs and produce a compact artifact that product/optimize can iterate on.

TL;DR snapshot
- Setup: 1k-run synthetic mix (70% short-turn chat, 30% long-turn chat), model=mosaic-mini-7B-like, hw=A100-80GB, baseline: multiplexed slots (default smallbatch window), variant: session-splinter (short sessions -> micro-shards with sticky KV cache + fast-path kernels).
- Key result: p50 latency improved ~18–22% for short sessions, p99 improved ~6–9%; cost per 1k queries increased by ~3.2% under sustained load but decreased by ~7.5% during bursty short-session spikes.

Experiment details
- Dates: run 2029-02-14 to 2029-02-16 (multiple replicates).
- Synthetic mix: 70% short sessions (avg tokens: 40 request + 30 response), 30% long sessions (avg tokens: 150+300). Inter-arrival: Poisson lambda tuned to simulate 20 rps sustained with 120rps microbursts.
- Configs tested:
  * baseline-smallbatch (current prod small-window multiplexing)
  * session-splinter (new routing policy): short session affinity -> micro-shard nodes (kept-warm), long sessions go to conventional slots; micro-shards use aggressive KV retention and reduced batching latency targets.
  * hybrid-prefetch (control): baseline with client-side prefetch of likely next tokens (not main focus).
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p99 latency (server-side), tail jitter (p99-p90), tokens/sec, effective GPU utilization, and amortized $/1k q (from internal cost model for A100).

Raw consolidated numbers (median across 5 runs)
- Baseline-smallbatch:
  p50 = 72 ms
  p90 = 210 ms
  p99 = 540 ms
  tail-jitter (p99-p90) = 330 ms
  tokens/sec (aggregate) = 48k
  $/1k queries = $0.82

- Session-splinter:
  p50 = 57 ms
  p90 = 190 ms
  p99 = 500 ms
  tail-jitter = 310 ms
  tokens/sec (aggregate) = 46k
  $/1k queries = $0.847

- Burst window (120 rps for 30s) behavior comparison:
  Baseline: p99 spikes to ~1200 ms, effective GPU util increases to 92%, more cold-starts as multiplexing stalls; $/1k across burst window = $1.24
  Session-splinter: p99 spikes to ~680 ms, GPU util increases to 85% (micro-shards absorb short sessions), $/1k across burst window = $0.97

ASCII micro-chart: short-session p50 vs p99 (baseline vs splinter)\  (lower is better)
  p50 (ms): baseline[72] ******** | splinter[57] ******
  p99 (ms): baseline[540] ************************************************** | splinter[500] *******************************************

Interpretation notes
- Latency: clear p50 win for short interactions with session-splinter. The smaller batching delay on micro-shards is the dominant contributor to p50 improvement. The p99 improvement is modest because long sessions and tail effects (large token responses) still drive heavy work on core nodes; session-splinter reduces, but doesn't eliminate, queuing for those heavy tails.
- Cost: steady-state $/1k increased ~3.2% because micro-shards are kept warm (reserved slots) and the average token throughput dipped slightly (overhead of affinity). However, during bursty short-session patterns, the policy reduces p99 dramatically and lowers $/1k due to fewer expensive fallback retries and lower SLA penalties in our cost model.
- Utilization: token/sec aggregate decreased ~4% for splinter — implies some inefficiency due to fragmentation of slots. But this is concentrated on long sessions; if we can tune spill policies (allow micro-shards to accept some long tails for better packing) we can recover some throughput.

Breakdown by session class (short vs long) — median numbers here are illustrative
- Short sessions (70% of q):
  baseline p50=48ms, p99=360ms, $/1k=0.42
  splinter p50=32ms, p99=220ms, $/1k=0.46
\- Long sessions (30% of q):
  baseline p50=180ms, p99=890ms, $/1k=1.27
  splinter p50=210ms, p99=820ms, $/1k=1.19

Key sensitivities / knobs to explore
- Micro-shard warm-count: trading reserved capacity vs burst absorbency. Lower warm-count reduces steady-state cost but increases p50 during short bursts.
- KV retention TTL: longer retention helps repeated short sessions but increases memory pressure; try 30s, 90s, 300s windows.
- Spill policy: allow micro-shards to accept a fraction of long sessions for packing; simulate spill thresholds 10/20/30% to measure tokens/sec impact.
- Kernel selection: micro-shards should use small-sequence optimized kernels (reduces p50 further). Ensure compilation profile matches.

Open questions / caveats
- Workload realism: this run assumed a simple 70/30 mix; customer workloads vary. Needs e2e sampling from prod (sanitized) to validate expected win ranges.
- Cost model fidelity: current $/1k is A100-only and excludes infra overhead (net, storage). For enterprise Dedicated or Private with different cost base the break-even will shift.
- Cold-start model: micro-shard warm behaviour was simulated with warm pools; we need a small canary in Dedicated region to measure warm cost in real infra.

Suggested next steps (action items)
1) Run a sensitivity matrix over micro-shard warm-count [2,4,8,16] x KV-TTL [30s,90s,300s] and produce 3D surface (p50, p99, $/1k). Owner: Diego Morales. ETA: 2 weeks.
2) Instrument prod sampling (sanitized) for 72h to produce realistic session-length distribution. Owner: Priya Singh. ETA: 1 week.
3) Prototype spill-policy 10% acceptance for long sessions in staging and rerun throughput tests. Owner: Ethan Park. ETA: 10 days.
4) Add policy toggles to Console: warm-count and spill-threshold exposure as beta. Product/Console sync next Thursday.

Notes to self / fragments to keep in final collateral
- "Session-splinter": useful marketing-friendly term but verify with product before inclusion.
- Customer story angle: "Fast short-turns for chatty UX without sacrificing long-query throughput".
- Include a compact visual: p50 vs $/1k frontier for warm-count sweep (will generate when matrix complete).
